title: 29. The Charity of the Head
purpose: It compiles the doctrinal rulings on zakat al-fitr (the charity of the head) — its substance, measure, timing, who owes it and on whose behalf — from the Pillars, fatwa collections and Ismaili authorities, closing with two edge-case rulings on ordinary zakat.

points.text: A fatwa collection arranged by the chapters of the Book of the Pillars addresses the Indian custom of mixing four grains (rice, maize, wheat, salt) for the fitra and taking their monetary value, and answers that the reliance is on the Pillars: a sa of wheat, barley, dates or raisins.
A transmitted saying holds that the fitra should be from the best of what one eats and the purest of what one stores.
The answer concedes latitude: whoever mixes his fitra from everything he ate during Ramadan has discharged it, and whoever ate nothing but barley may give barley.

On paying the fitra before Ramadan out of fear of poverty or travel — objected to because obligatory acts may not be done outside their appointed times — the answer is that delivering it to a rightful recipient suffices, since no fixed time was set for advancing or delaying it and the obligation is simply its delivery; the only prohibition is that one not break the fast before delivering it.
Mukhtasar al-Musannaf rules that a dhimmi who accepts Islam before dawn on the day of Fitr owes the zakat of Fitr, while one who converts after dawn owes nothing.

Reports state the zakat of Fitr is paid for the mukatab; the Landmarks of Religion holds it due for a child born before dawn on the day of Fitr; and the Book of the Pillars records that it has also been said to be paid for a child still in the womb.

The measure of the sa is given as four and a half ratls by the Meccan ratl, five ratls less a third by the Medinan ratl, and nine and a tenth by the Baghdadi ratl, with the Selected Book allowing a sa of dried curd or half a sa of wheat.

The author of the Mustansiriyya sessions, in the thirteenth session, distinguishes zakat obligatory on the wealthy from zakat of Fitr, which is obligatory in every condition and even on those of small means, and enumerates seven obligations — that a man pay it for himself, for the elder and younger of his household, the free and the enslaved, the males and the females — plus twelve Sunnah practices.

Among the Sunnah practices: it is brought out from the middle sort of one's food — a sa of wheat, barley, dates or raisins, with half a sa sufficing only for wheat; the sa is four mudds; it is handed to the Imam or his appointee before the breaking of the fast; delay requires making it up; one lacking food gives its value in silver or gold; and a woman without a husband pays for herself and her dependents.
The Inner Nursing cites the Prophet's saying that the fitra is not lawful for him nor for the people of his house.

Zayd ibn Muhammad's Concealed Epistle states that the Messenger of God made the fitra obligatory on every head among the Muslims — male and female, small and great, even an infant born that day and the child in the womb — a sa of wheat, dates, raisins, barley or other grain, which is why it is named the charity of the head; if paid before the prayer it counts as charity.

Al-Qadi al-Numan's Mafatih al-Nima draws the temporal distinction that what is brought out before sunrise counts as fitra and after sunrise as ordinary charity, and defines the meaning of fitra as bringing out what is owed to God and to His appointed guardian, as ransom and as offering.

Two puzzle-rulings close the section: a man owning a thousand dinars while owing a thousand dinars owes no zakat on it, and a polytheist who finds no Muslim to whom to hand his zakat has more right to it than anyone else.
